entry.title: Set the URL beside the mark rather than under it
entry.content:
Set the URL beside the mark rather than under it

Both go in the one h2 with `align="middle"` on the image, so the link
sits vertically centred against the wordmark and GitHub's heading rule
runs under the pair. Compared against a float and an inline plain link
under GitHub's own stylesheet; the float does not hold its rule, and a
body-weight link beside a 265px mark reads as a caption.

`align` is one of the few layout attributes GitHub's sanitiser keeps —
`style` is not, so there is no flexbox route to this.

entry.title: Review the README end to end
entry.content:
Review the README end to end

Going public makes this the front door, so every claim in it wanted
checking against the code. Three were wrong or stale.

- The built-in decks section was written as though they start visible.
  `DEFAULT_PREFS` has `showBuiltIns: false`, so the index opens empty.
  Reframed, and the intro now says so rather than promising twelve decks
  to someone about to meet an empty screen
- "Thirteen study and print routes" is thirteen slugs on each of two
  route trees, so twenty-six
- The file tree omitted `new/page.tsx`, the importer and the generator
  while the prose discussed all three at length

Adds what was missing: the deck generator, which is a real feature
touching the reader's own API key and had no mention at all; the build,
lint and test commands; and a Storage section that names the four
localStorage keys and is honest that browsers clear them.

Also folds "imported decks live in one browser" into Storage, where it
belongs beside the same caveat for progress.

entry.title: Widen the index headline and lift the footer off the grid
entry.content:
Widen the index headline and lift the footer off the grid

Measured on a 1512px desktop, where the headline was breaking earlier
than it needed to and the footer sat too close to the grid above it.

- h1 to 40rem, so "when you add one:" stays on the first line
- lead paragraph to 33rem, one rem past max-w-lg, which lands the wrap
  after "the part"
- the footer row to 100px of clearance, as `sm:mt-25`

Neither max-width binds below its own value, so both are no-ops on a
phone. The margin would not be: 100px of dead space above the fold on a
375px screen is a lot, so it is held at the existing 40px until the sm
breakpoint.

entry.title: Replan TASKS.md around spaced repetition
entry.content:
Replan TASKS.md around spaced repetition

Adds the seven tasks that bring Leitner scheduling to the reviewer, and
regroups the file now that it holds two unrelated tracks.

The scheduling tasks are ordered and interdependent: one progress store,
boxes and due dates, the queue builder, the reviewer studying the queue,
due counts, the cross-deck due queue, docs. Task 1 is worth landing on
its own merits — `progress:all` and `progress:{slug}` hold the same
`{deckSlug}:{cardId}` key with different values today, so a draft written
on one route reads as empty on the other.

Removes tasks 1 and 2, both long since shipped, and defers "in rotation"
to Not now. Rotation is postponed as premature rather than dropped: it
scopes by goal where the due queue scopes by time, and you cannot tell
whether the queue needs a goal filter until you have lived with one that
has none.

Records two rejected options in Not now so they are not rediscovered:
progress export/import, and the rotation deferral above.

entry.title: Start with the built-in decks off
entry.content:
Start with the built-in decks off

The decks in content/ are mine, and somebody arriving at this app has
not asked for them. DEFAULT_PREFS now says so: showBuiltIns is false,
and loadPrefs takes only a stored true for an answer, so a missing or
half-written value reads as a first visit rather than as consent. A
reader who ever pressed the switch has their choice stored either way,
so the new default only ever describes somebody who has not made one.

That default is also what the server prerenders, which is what lets the
pre-paint script in app/layout.tsx go. It had a job only while the
server rendered decks the reader did not want: it hid them before they
could flash. The index now renders no built-in grid at all, so there is
nothing to paint and then take away, and the grid arrives with the
preferences the same way the imported decks always have. The `built-ins`
class and the data-deck attributes go with it, being the selectors it
wrote and nothing else read. CLAUDE.md records why it existed, so it
comes back if the default is ever flipped again.

The trade is the mirror of the old one: a reader who has turned the
decks on sees them appear on hydration. That is the smaller flicker,
and it falls on somebody who has chosen the decks rather than on
everybody who has not.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Turn the mark into a sun on the index
entry.content:
Turn the mark into a sun on the index

A WebGL sunburst behind the wordmark: twenty rays out of the mark's own
frame, turning clockwise, a full circuit every three minutes or so.
They are one flat colour — the mark's cream, a fifth of the way from
the paper — so the whole figure is two tones and a clean edge, cut
rather than faded.

Rendered by app/page.tsx rather than by the layout, so the shader and
its loop stay in the index's chunk: a page you have come to in order to
study should not have something moving at the top of it, nor carry the
code for it. The canvas is fixed and full-window on a negative
z-index, which is what the shell's new `relative z-10` is for — it
opens the stacking context that keeps the canvas behind the page and
still in front of the paper.

The rays leave a rounded rectangle six pixels outside the mark's frame,
using the frame's own corner radius from tools/wordmark.py so the hole
stays the shape of the thing it is a hole for. Colours come from the
theme, --color-mark being the cream the mark is printed on.

Written premultiplied, to match how the canvas is composited: straight
alpha turned every softened pixel white rather than a step between the
two tones. Reduced motion keeps the light and drops the rotation.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Separate the cards the export writes, and only pin an overriding ink
entry.content:
Separate the cards the export writes, and only pin an overriding ink

toDeckText joined its cards with a single newline, so every card's
`id:` landed directly under the answer above it — the exact shape the
parser used to misread, and the origin of the decks in content/ that
carry it. A deck exported from the app is what gets kept and read back,
so the two ends have to agree. There is a blank line between the cards
now.

`ink:` was left out of the front matter altogether, though it is a
required field on a Deck and the parser reads it. Exporting a built-in
deck lost the colour its text and progress bars are drawn in. It is
written now, but only when the tint would not give it: an ink is
derived from its tint's hue, and writing one for every deck would
freeze today's shade into decks that are meant to keep tracking
shadeForTint. The four that do carry one are the built-ins, whose inks
came from the print spec and sit up to 21 points of saturation and 20
of lightness off the formula, in both directions.

The round-trip test alone would not have held any of this: with the
parser now reading a uuid id line mid-answer, the old export parses
back correctly too. The cases that bite assert on the exported text.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Read a card id that follows an answer directly
entry.content:
Read a card id that follows an answer directly

An `id:` line was only recognised when the parser was not part-way
through an answer, so that an answer happening to begin "id:" stayed
part of that answer. But `field` only clears on a blank line, and eight
of the decks in content/ are written with none between their cards, so
every id after the first arrived mid-answer: it was appended to the
answer above it, and the card it belonged to was given a generated one
instead.

That is not cosmetic. loadDecks parses at build time, so those cards
were rekeyed on every build, and progress is kept by card id. On
next-js-app-router.md, 1 id of 24 came from the file and 23 changed on
every parse.

An id line whose value is a uuid now closes the card above it wherever
it appears. A non-uuid still stays in the answer, which is the case the
guard was there for.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
